summary: A landlocked country on the Indochinese Peninsula, traversed by the Mekong River, once the site of the Kingdom of Lan Xang; in 1975 the socialist Lao People's Democratic Republic was established.

ranking.name: Theravada Buddhism
ranking.description: In the 14th century Fa Ngum, founder of the Kingdom of Lan Xang, brought back the Phra Bang Buddha image from Cambodia and promoted Theravada Buddhism, and Buddhism has since been the state religion of the Lao; in the 16th century King Setthathirath also built That Luang in Vientiane. Today the Buddhist believers are mainly the Lao and Tai peoples living in the lowlands along the Mekong, and temporary ordination of men and the daily giving of sticky rice to monks remain part of everyday life. After the communist regime was established in 1975 Buddhism was restricted, but after the 1990s the attitude turned supportive.

ranking.name: Folk religion (animism)
ranking.description: Laos has about 50 officially recognized ethnic groups, and many highland peoples such as the Hmong, Khmu and Akha have never accepted Buddhism and still believe in ancestral spirits, nature spirits and shamanic healing. These peoples mostly live in the mountain regions of the north and south, with poor transport and little influence from the state and Buddhist culture, so the share of folk religion is very high.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced by missionaries during the French colonial period of 1893–1953, and believers are mostly in cities and in the Vietnamese-descended community. Protestantism spread in the 20th century among some highland peoples. The communist government is relatively wary of Christianity, and incidents of forcing believers to renounce their faith have occurred in rural areas.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: This includes a small number of Muslims (mostly merchants of South Asian and Cham descent), the Baha'i Faith, and Chinese folk religion and Mahayana Buddhism.

religion.background: When Fa Ngum founded the Kingdom of Lan Xang in the 14th century, the lowland Lao of Laos introduced Theravada Buddhism from Angkor and enshrined the Phra Bang Buddha image, and Buddhism became the core of royal authority and national identity. The highland minorities long kept their beliefs in ancestral spirits and animism, and even Lao Buddhists commonly make offerings to spirits called "phi". Catholicism was introduced during French colonial rule in 1893–1953. After the Lao People's Revolutionary Party established its communist regime in 1975, the activities of monks were for a time restricted, but from the late 1980s the government turned to using Buddhism to build national identity, and That Luang was even placed on the national emblem.

ranking.name: Lao
ranking.description: The Lao are Laos's most numerous ethnic group, living mainly in the lowlands along the Mekong, and the Lao language has been the language of the court and of Buddhism since the Lan Xang period. After 1975 the government made Lao the sole official language and extended it to all schools, so even though only about half the population has it as a mother tongue, most minorities can communicate in Lao as a second language.

ranking.name: Hmong
ranking.description: The Hmong moved into the mountains of northern Laos from southwestern China in the 19th century. During the Vietnam War many Hmong were recruited by the CIA to take part in the "Secret War" against communist forces, and after the communist victory in 1975 large numbers of Hmong fled to refugee camps in Thailand and later emigrated to the United States and elsewhere. The Hmong who stayed in Laos still use Hmong as their main language, concentrated in northern provinces such as Xiangkhouang and Luang Prabang.

language.history: Lao belongs to the Tai branch of the Kra-Dai family and is very close to Thai (especially the Isan language of northeastern Thailand); the ancestors of the Lao migrated south from what is now southern China to the Mekong basin around the 8th–13th centuries. The Lao script derives from the Khmer script, gradually took shape after the Lan Xang period in the 14th century, and was first used to write Buddhist scriptures. During the French colonial period of 1893–1953 French became the language of administration; after the communist regime was established in 1975, a script reform simplified the spelling, and Lao was promoted as the national language to all ethnic groups. Today minorities in the mountains still widely use their own languages, while Lao serves as the national lingua franca.

ranking.name: Larb (minced meat salad)
ranking.description: A "minced meat salad" in which chopped meat or fish is mixed with lime juice, fish sauce, chili, toasted rice powder, mint and coriander. It tastes sour, spicy, salty and fragrant, and is often eaten with sticky rice and raw vegetables.
ranking.history: Larb is regarded as the national dish of Laos, and in Lao it sounds like the word for "good luck", so it always appears at joyous occasions such as weddings, the New Year (the water festival in April) and house-warmings. It comes from the food tradition of the Lao, and the Isan region of northeastern Thailand (whose inhabitants are mostly of Lao descent) is also famous for larb. Traditionally it can be made with raw meat, with toasted rice powder added for aroma and texture, a distinctive seasoning technique of the Lao.

ranking.name: Sticky rice (khao niao)
ranking.localName: ເຂົ້າໜຽວ (Khao niao)
ranking.description: Glutinous rice is soaked and steamed in a bamboo basket, then pinched by hand into small balls to dip into dishes; it is the daily staple of Lao people. It is chewy and springy, and eaten with various sauces and dishes.
ranking.history: Laos is the country with the highest share of glutinous rice consumption in the world, the Lao have grown glutinous rice for over a thousand years, and they even call themselves "children of sticky rice" (luk khao niao). Sticky rice is filling, easy to carry, and suited to mountain and field labor. Every early morning in places such as Luang Prabang, the faithful place sticky rice into the bowls of monks as alms, and this "alms round" ritual is the most representative sight of Lao Buddhist culture.

ranking.name: Green papaya salad (tam mak hoong)
ranking.localName: ຕຳໝາກຫຸ່ງ (Tam mak hoong)
ranking.description: A sour and spicy salad in which shredded green papaya is pounded in a mortar with chili, garlic, lime juice, fish sauce and fermented fish sauce (padaek).
ranking.history: Papaya is native to the Americas and reached Southeast Asia around the 16th century and after via Portuguese and Spanish trade, and the Lao combined it with their traditional pounded-dish technique. The Lao version notably adds the strongly flavored fermented fish sauce padaek, and compared with Thailand's som tam it is saltier and more robust. It is the side dish and snack Lao people eat most in daily life, often paired with sticky rice and grilled chicken.

ranking.name: Lao rice noodle soup (khao piak sen)
ranking.localName: ເຂົ້າປຽກເສັ້ນ (Khao piak sen)
ranking.description: Chewy thick noodles made from rice flour and tapioca starch are put in a thick chicken-bone broth, served with chicken, fried garlic and herbs.
ranking.history: Khao piak sen means "wet rice noodles", because the batter noodles release starch as they cook in the broth, making it thick. It is similar to Vietnam's bánh canh, reflecting the long cultural exchange between Laos and Vietnam. In Laos it is a common breakfast and late-night meal, especially popular in the cool rainy season and in the mountains.

ranking.name: Or lam (Lao stew)
ranking.localName: ເອາະຫລາມ (Or lam)
ranking.description: A thick stew of water buffalo meat or game stewed with eggplant, yardlong beans, chili, dill and a pungent woody plant (sakhan).
ranking.history: Or lam is a representative dish of Luang Prabang and is thought to come from the court cuisine of the Kingdom of Lan Xang. The sakhan in it (the stem of a pepper vine), when sliced, produces a numbing, spicy sensation in the mouth, a hallmark of Luang Prabang cooking. In the past it was often made with hunted game, reflecting the mountain and forest life of northern Laos. After Luang Prabang was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1995, this dish also became representative for visitors getting to know traditional Lao cuisine.
